title: Acting
subtitle: Strong poses, blinks, eye darts, takes and breathing

lessons.title: Line of Action
lessons.summary: Strong poses flow along one line.

steps.title: One strong line
steps.text: The orange line is the line of action: one clear line through the whole body.

beats.say: Every strong pose starts with one simple line through the whole body. It's called the line of action.
This one's stiff. A straight line, straight up and down. It's not wrong, it just feels a bit flat.
Now a C curve. The back bends, the head leans in, and suddenly there's energy in it.
An S curve flows one way, then the other. It feels relaxed and graceful, like a dancer.
So when you start a pose, draw the line first. Then hang the body on it.

steps.title: Draw the line of action
steps.text: Trace one big, confident C curve. This is where a pose starts.
steps.hint: One smooth sweep, from bottom to top. Don't stop halfway.

steps.title: Pose to pose
steps.text: Three poses on three frames: stiff, then a C curve, then an S curve. Draw the line first, then the body on it.
steps.hint: Draw the back line first on every frame. The head, arms and legs follow it.
tips: Stiff. A straight back, head right on top. Draw the line, then the limbs.
The C curve. Bend the back into one big curve and lean the head into it.
The S curve. The back bends one way, then the other, like a wave.

quiz.question: Which line of action has the most energy?
choices: A curvy C or S line
quiz.explain: Curves feel alive; straight lines feel stiff.

lessons.title: Blinks
lessons.summary: A blink is quick to close and a little slower to open.

steps.title: Break down a blink
steps.text: A natural blink, frame by frame.

beats.say: A blink is one of the easiest ways to make a character feel alive. Let's watch one.
It closes really fast. Just one in-between, and then it's shut.
It stays shut for a frame or two. Any longer and it starts to look sleepy.
Then it opens a bit slower than it closed. Two in-betweens on the way up.
See how the top lid does almost all the moving? The bottom lid hardly moves at all.
And here's a pro touch. The brows dip down a little as the eyes close, then lift back up.
Blink when a character changes their mind, turns their head, or every few seconds while they listen.

steps.title: Animate a blink
steps.text: Six frames, with the holds already set. Draw both eyes and brows on every frame.
steps.hint: The top lid comes down to meet the bottom one. The brows dip a little when the eyes shut.
tips: Eyes open, looking straight ahead. Brows relaxed.
Half closed. The top lids slide down past the pupils.
Shut. Just two curved lines, and the brows dip down a touch.
Starting to open. The top lids lift a little.
Nearly open. The pupils peek back out.
Open again, brows back where they started.

quiz.question: Which is faster in a normal blink?
quiz.explain: Eyes snap shut quickly, then open a little slower.

quiz.question: When is a great moment to add a blink?
choices: When a character turns their head or has a new thought
In the middle of a big shout
quiz.explain: Blinks mark a change, like a new thought or a head turn.

lessons.title: Eyes Lead the Way
lessons.summary: The eyes move first, then the head follows.

steps.title: Eyes first, head second
steps.text: Something catches their eye on the right.

beats.say: Something just caught this character's attention, over on the right. Watch what moves first.
The eyes. They dart across in a single frame. Real eyes jump like that, no in-betweens.
Then they hold for a moment. That little pause is the character noticing something.
Now the head turns to follow, easing in and out. Everything on the face slides across together.
And there's a blink right in the middle of the turn. It hides the jump and feels really natural.
By the end, the head has caught up, so the eyes drift back toward the middle.
Eyes lead, the head follows, then the body. Remember that order and your acting will feel real.

steps.title: Animate the eye dart and head turn
steps.text: Six frames: look, dart, turn, blink, turn, settle. Draw the eyes, brows, nose and mouth on every frame. The head circle is already there.
steps.hint: The pupils jump first. On the blink frame, the eyes are just two curves.
tips: Looking straight ahead. Pupils in the middle, face in the middle.
The dart. Only the pupils move, right over to the right side.
The head starts turning. Slide the whole face a little to the right.
Blink in the middle of the turn. The eyes are closed curves.
Eyes open again, the face nearly all the way round.
The head's caught up. The pupils drift back toward the middle.

quiz.question: When a character notices something, what moves first?
quiz.explain: Eyes lead, then the head, then the body.

quiz.question: Why put a blink in the middle of a head turn?
choices: It feels natural and hides the jump
quiz.explain: People really do blink as they turn, so it reads as natural.

lessons.title: The Take
lessons.summary: A big surprised reaction: squash, stretch, hold, settle.

steps.title: Break down a take
steps.text: A cartoon double take, worked out as squash and stretch on the whole head.

beats.say: This is a take. It's how a cartoon character reacts to a big surprise. Watch the whole thing.
First, anticipation. The head squashes down, the eyes squeeze shut, the brows push down.
Then, pop! It stretches up tall. Brows shoot up, eyes go huge, the mouth drops open.
Now hold it. The audience needs a moment to read the expression. Don't rush this part.
Then it settles back down, but stays a little surprised. It doesn't snap back to calm.
Squash before, stretch for the hit, hold, then settle. The bigger the squash, the bigger the take.

steps.title: Animate a take
steps.text: Five key poses with the holds already set. Draw the head shape and the face on every frame.
steps.hint: The head stays the same size overall. Squashed is short and wide, stretched is tall and thin.
tips: Calm. A round head, relaxed brows, a soft closed mouth.
Anticipation. Squash the head short and wide, eyes squeezed, brows down.
The take! Stretch the head tall and thin, huge eyes, brows way up, mouth open.
Hold. Still surprised, just a little less stretched.
Settle. Nearly round again, eyes still big, mouth a small O.

quiz.question: What comes right before the big stretch of a take?
quiz.explain: The squash is the anticipation that makes the stretch pop.

quiz.question: Why hold the take for a moment?
choices: So the audience can read the expression
quiz.explain: A held pose gives people time to see the feeling.

lessons.title: Breathing & Moving Holds
lessons.summary: A still character is never totally frozen.

steps.title: Alive, even when still
steps.text: A gentle breathing loop: the body rises and falls a tiny bit.

beats.say: Even when a character is just standing there, they're breathing. Watch the top of the bean.
Breathing in, the body stretches up a little and gets slimmer.
Breathing out, it settles back down and gets a touch wider.
It's tiny. If you can really see it, it's too much. It should feel alive, not like it's bouncing.
Animators call this a moving hold. Use it whenever a character holds a pose for more than a second.

steps.title: Animate a breathing loop
steps.text: Eight frames that loop. Draw the bean on every frame, rising and falling just a little.
steps.hint: Keep the feet on the ground. Only the top rises and falls.
tips: The middle of the breath. The normal bean.
Breathing in. A tiny bit taller and slimmer.
The top of the breath. The tallest it gets.
Starting to breathe out. Coming back down.
Back to the middle again.
Breathing out. A tiny bit shorter and wider.
The bottom of the breath. The shortest it gets.
Coming back up. Then it loops to frame 1.

quiz.question: A character holds still for three seconds. You should...
choices: Keep a tiny bit of movement, like breathing
quiz.explain: A moving hold keeps them looking alive.
